title: Forgotten Depths - A Smallish Game in a GIANT BOX!
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TWUoFcCtDhA

Daniel (@dungeondive) returns to *Forgotten Depths* now that the Kickstarter has delivered, and splits the video deliberately: the game first, the packaging second, because his feelings about the two could not be further apart.

The design he walks through as five small twists on familiar verbs. You build the floor as a tile-laying puzzle before deciding what to encounter. Open-circle nodes must be connected into shapes — a straight pair, an L, something harder — and each shape unlocks a tier of legendary location. Doors, monsters and features block progress in their direction, so the order of encounters is yours to sequence. Combat is card columns with automatic return damage equal to the difference, making a big swing genuinely risky. Each hero has a personal loot deck that dresses them in their own iconic gear. Marin Churchland's soft, muted, almost pastoral art gives the whole thing a chill and inviting vibe he adores.

Then the box. The rulebook is newspaper-sized, floppy, with tiny type and pages three-fifths blank. The box is nearly as large as *Stars of Akarios* for a small card game, and the contents fit inside a *Paper Dungeons* box with room to spare. He blames the absence of anyone on a Kickstarter empowered to say no, and takes the plastic insert as a broader industry problem.

----

Does an obnoxious box and rulebook legitimately count against a game you otherwise love, or is that a complaint about the publisher rather than the design?
